'''Charles Norwood Reilley''' (March 2, 1925 – December 31, 1981) was an American chemist known for his contributions to [[analytical chemistry]], particularly in [[electrochemistry]], chemical instrumentation, and the development of modern quantitative methods. He was a professor at the [[University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill]] and was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 1977.<ref name=NASmemoir>{{cite book |last=Murray |first=Royce W. |title=Charles Norwood Reilley, 1925–1981 |series=Biographical Memoirs of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=88 |publisher=National Academies Press |year=2006 |url=https://www.nasonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/reilley-charles.pdf}}</ref><ref name=NASdirectory>{{cite web |title=Charles Norwood Reilley |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/charles-reilley-yqdvzo/ |publisher=National Academy of Sciences |access-date=27 March 2026}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Reilley was born in Charlotte, North Carolina. His father died when he was young, and he was raised by his mother, a public school teacher.<ref name=NCpedia>{{cite web |last=Bursey |first=Maurice M. |title=Reilley, Charles Norwood |url=https://www.ncpedia.org/biography/reilley-charles-norwood |publisher=NCpedia |year=1994}}</ref> He developed an early interest in electronics and science, which led him to pursue chemistry.<ref name=NCpedia />

He received a B.S. in chemistry from the [[University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill]] in 1947, followed by an M.A. (1951) and Ph.D. (1952) from [[Princeton University]], where he worked under analytical chemist [[N. Howell Furman]].<ref name=NASmemoir />

== Career ==

After completing his doctorate, Reilley returned to the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, where he spent his entire academic career. He rose through the ranks from instructor to professor and was appointed Kenan Professor in 1963.<ref name=NASmemoir />

Reilley played a role in modernizing chemical education, advocating for the early integration of instrumental analysis into undergraduate curricula. His reforms helped establish UNC as an institution for undergraduate chemistry education in the 1960s and 1970s.<ref name=NASmemoir />

He was widely regarded as a teacher and mentor, known for his ability to engage colleagues and students alike in intellectually stimulating discussions that advanced their understanding of science.<ref name=Isenhour1982>{{cite journal |last=Isenhour |first=Thomas L. |title=Charles Norwood Reilley, March 2, 1925–December 31, 1981 |journal=Analytical Chemistry |year=1982 |volume=54 |issue=3 |pages=426A–431A |doi=10.1021/ac00240a718}}</ref>

Over the course of his career, he made contributions across multiple areas of analytical chemistry, including electrochemistry, chromatography, complexation chemistry, nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, and laboratory automation.<ref name=Isenhour1982 />

== Research and contributions ==
* [[Electrochemistry]] and [[Titration|titrimetry]]: He developed theoretical models for electrochemical detection methods, including high-frequency titrimetry and coulometric titrations, and designed instrumentation for precise current control.<ref name=NASmemoir /><ref name=Reilley1951>{{cite journal |last1=Furman |first1=N. H. |last2=Cooke |first2=W. D. |last3=Reilley |first3=C. N. |title=Coulometric titrations with electrically generated ceric ion |journal=Analytical Chemistry |year=1951 |volume=23 |issue=7 |pages=945–946 |doi=10.1021/ac60055a004}}</ref><ref name=Reilley1953>{{cite journal |last1=Reilley |first1=C. N. |last2=McCurdy |first2=W. H. Jr. |title=Principles of high-frequency titrimetry |journal=Analytical Chemistry |year=1953 |volume=25 |issue=1 |pages=86–93 |doi=10.1021/ac60073a014}}</ref>
* [[Metal complex]] chemistry: He advanced understanding of metal–ligand equilibria, including the thermodynamic basis of the chelate effect, and developed widely used analytical reagents and methods for metal ion detection.<ref name=NASmemoir /><ref name=Reilley1965Chelate>{{cite journal |last1=Wright |first1=D. L. |last2=Holloway |first2=J. H. |last3=Reilley |first3=C. N. |title=Heat and entropies of formation of metal chelates of polyamine and polyaminocarboxylate ligands |journal=Analytical Chemistry |year=1965 |volume=37 |issue=7 |pages=884–892 |doi=10.1021/ac60226a025}}</ref>
* [[Spectroscopy]] and [[NMR]]: He pioneered the use of nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy to study metal complexes and protonation equilibria.<ref name=NASmemoir /><ref name=Reilley1964NMR>{{cite journal |last1=Sudmeier |first1=J. L. |last2=Reilley |first2=C. N. |title=Nuclear magnetic resonance studies of protonation of polyamine and aminocarboxylate compounds in aqueous solution |journal=Analytical Chemistry |year=1964 |volume=36 |issue=9 |pages=1698–1706 |doi=10.1021/ac60215a006}}</ref>
* [[Chromatography]] and separations: He contributed to developments in gas–liquid chromatography and related analytical separation and kinetic methods.<ref name=NASmemoir /><ref name=Reilley1964GLC>{{cite journal |last1=Hildebrand |first1=G. P. |last2=Reilley |first2=C. N. |title=Use of combination columns in gas liquid chromatography |journal=Analytical Chemistry |year=1964 |volume=36 |issue=1 |pages=47–58 |doi=10.1021/ac60207a019}}</ref>
* [[Chemometrics]] and computing: He was among the first to apply pattern recognition and early computational methods to chemical data, helping to establish the field of chemometrics.<ref name=NASmemoir /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jurs |first1=P. C. |last2=Kowalski |first2=B. R. |last3=Isenhour |first3=Thomas L. |last4=Reilley |first4=C. N. |title=Computerized learning machines applied to chemical problems. Convergence rate and predictive ability of adaptive binary pattern classifiers |journal=Analytical Chemistry |year=1969 |volume=41 |issue=6 |pages=690–695 |doi=10.1021/ac60275a025}}</ref>

Reilley also developed practical analytical tools, including a galvanic electrode for measuring dissolved oxygen in natural waters, which was widely adopted in environmental chemistry.<ref name=NASmemoir /><ref name=Reilley1962Oxygen>{{cite journal |last1=Mancy |first1=K. H. |last2=Okun |first2=D. A. |last3=Reilley |first3=C. N. |title=A galvanic cell oxygen analyzer |journal=Journal of Electroanalytical Chemistry |year=1962 |volume=4 |issue=2 |pages=65–92 |doi=10.1016/0022-0728(62)80035-7}}</ref>

== Honors and awards ==
* [[American Chemical Society]] Award in Analytical Chemistry (Fisher Award, 1965)<ref name=NASmemoir />
* [[Herty Medal]] (1968)<ref name=NASmemoir />
* Charles H. Stone Award (1971)<ref name=NASmemoir />
* ANACHEM Award (1972)<ref name=NASmemoir />
* Manufacturing Chemists Association College Chemistry Teaching Award (1975)<ref name=NASmemoir />
* In 1977, he was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref name="NASmemoir" />

== Legacy ==

Following his death in 1981, the Society for Electroanalytical Chemistry established the Charles N. Reilley Award in electroanalytical chemistry in his honor, first awarded in 1984.<ref>{{cite web |title=Charles N. Reilley Award |url=https://seac.online/awards/reilley-award/ |publisher=Society for Electroanalytical Chemistry |access-date=27 March 2026}}</ref>
